bib.title: Towards System 2 Reasoning in LLMs: Learning How to Think With Meta Chain-of-Thought

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Towards System 2 Reasoning in LLMs: Learning How to Think With Meta Chain-of-Thought", Violet Xiang, Charlie Snell, Kanishk Gandhi, Alon Albalak, Anikait Singh, Chase Blagden, Duy Phung, Rafael Rafailov, Nathan Lile, Dakota Mahan, Louis Castricato, Jan-Philipp Franken, Nick Haber, Chelsea Finn (SynthLabs, Stanford, UC Berkeley). Preprint (no venue printed), 2025; the paper calls itself "this position paper" (Sec 9). Dated by the file name, and it cites late-2024 work (o1, R1-lite-preview, QwQ).

COVERAGE: Read all of the 261,184-char extraction (4,581 lines): body, Sec 1-10, Appendices A-D, Table 5, reference list skimmed. The Appendix E raw reasoning traces (about lines 2940-4500, roughly 60 pages) were only skimmed for structure and the tail. They are model transcripts, not results. The pypdf warning "Impossible to decode XFormObject /Im21" is harmless. Equations and some figure text are garbled in the extraction.

IMPORTANT FRAMING FOR THE TARGET NOTE (07-prompting-reasoning-models): this is a theory and roadmap paper about training reasoning models. It is NOT a prompting guide. Only Sec 6.4.1 and Appendices A/B test prompting. Those are the claims most relevant to prompting reasoning models.

CLAIMS (ranked)
1. Prompting a non-reasoning model to "think, reflect, backtrack, verify" produces reasoning-like text but not reliably better answers.
 number: Plain baseline/CoT prompts show regret (explicit error acknowledgement) in <0.5% of solutions. Think prompt: 12.65% for Llama 3.1 70B. Think & Verify peaks at 25.67% (Llama 3.1 70B). Accuracy gains do not follow.
 setup: MATH test set; 5 prompt strategies (Baseline, CoT, Think, Think 3-shot, Think & Verify); Llama 3.1 8B/70B/405B, GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, GPT-3.5-turbo, Claude 3.5 Sonnet/Haiku. Regret = phrases such as "I made a mistake", "oops", "let me reconsider". The authors' own small study.
 quote: "Under baseline and standard CoT prompting, which provide no explicit instruction for self-verification, models rarely express regret or acknowledge errors (<0.5% of solutions across all models)" and "peaking at 25.67% for Llama 3.1 70B under the Think & Verify strategy."
 where: Sec 6.4.1, p38; Table 5, p~100 (offset ~4532)
2. More elaborate prompts cost many more tokens and do not give proportional accuracy.
 number: Think & Verify matches accuracy on the lowest difficulty "while often requiring more than double the token budget". Prompt overhead (input tokens, GPT-4o tokenizer): Baseline 23, CoT 35, Think 1,895, Think 3-shot 4,659, Think & Verify 2,111.
 setup: same MATH study; Table 4 in Appendix A.
 quote: "we find that the Think & Verify strategy leads to equivalent accuracies on the lowest difficulty problems (for all models), while often requiring more than double the token budget." Table 4 rows: "Think with demonstrations (3-shot) 4,659".
 where: p38-39; p62
3. Models imitate the style of reasoning, and when they backtrack the final answer is more likely wrong.
 number: none (qualitative; no figure given for the correlation)
 setup: same study; Llama 8B shows more tokens and lower accuracy on hard levels; larger models keep token use steadier.
 quote: "models seek to match the reasoning "style" rather than substance and may be even faking mistakes to match the desired in-context behaviors" and "when models engage in self-correction and backtracking, the final answers are more likely to be incorrect."
 where: p39
4. Regret rate scales with model size only non-monotonically: strong closed models express little.
 number: Llama 15-25% under Think & Verify; GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet 1-4%. Table 5: GPT-4o Think & Verify 1.52%, Claude 3.5 Sonnet 4.44%, Llama 3.1 8B 20.87%, 405B 15.67%.
 quote: "While larger Llama models show high rates of regret expression (15-25% under Think & Verify), more advanced models like GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet exhibit notably lower rates (1-4%)."
 where: p38
5. Authors' conclusion: prompting cannot induce real meta-reasoning; SFT on search traces plus RL is needed.
 quote: "we presented evidence that the current generation of models cannot induce effective meta-reasoning through in-context prompting, and may even exhibit misleading behaviors."
 where: Sec 7.1, p39
6. Core thesis (Meta-CoT): for hard problems the true data-generating process is a latent search, not left-to-right CoT; o1-like models spend more tokens as difficulty rises.
 number: none; evidence is HARP (Yue et al. 2024) token counts, figure sourced from that paper.
 quote: "outside of the o1 series of models, LLMs generate solutions of comparable lengths to humans" and "the gap between the inference compute used by the o1 model and prior series of models seems to scale with the complexity of the problems."
 where: Sec 2.2, p9
7. Sampling shows a large generator-verifier gap in an 8B model.
 number: pass@64 near 85%; maj@64 beats greedy using only 15% of the training compute; greedy goes from about 20% to 40%.
 setup: Llama 3.1 8B base, SFT on Numina MATH, evaluated on MATH-500. Authors call it a "preliminary study".
 quote: "the pass@64 for the final checkpoint of an 8B model achieves accuracy close to 85%, outperforming the zero-shot performance of many current frontier models" and "maj@64 outperforming the greedy model performance with only 15% of the training compute"
 where: p11
8. In-context revision scales better than parallel sampling.
 number: nearly 6-7% pass@1 gain from zero-shot to saturation (figure from Snell et al. 2024). Variable-compute replication: 2.45 solutions on average at Level 1 vs 5.84 at Level 5; best run only +2% over Llama 3.1 8B Instruct.
 setup: MATH, Llama 3.1 8B, up to 8 in-context solutions.
 quote: "the model generates an average of 2.45 solutions for Level 1 problems and an average of 5.84 for Level 5 problems" and "any regular SFT training we performed on the RL post-trained model actually worsened performance."
 where: p19-20
9. Evidence that RL finds new reasoning algorithms is weak; the gain is efficiency.
 number: the SoS model solves about 1% of Countdown problems that symbolic search cannot, RL-tuned up to 4%. Code at 70B, k=100: RL model "only about 5% above the base model".
 quote: "there is only weak evidence that these models can discover novel reasoning methods that can solve classes of problems that were not solvable previously under some search budget."
 where: Sec 6.3, p34-35
10. Standard RL with no in-context exploration generalizes worse; multi-turn training scales better.
 number: RLEF (Gehring et al. 2024) pass rates, 8B: Instruct 10.5 (test) -> SFT 10.0 -> RLEF 16.0; 70B: 27.5 -> 27.2 -> 40.1. The 1-turn RL model is worse than the base at high sample budgets; a 3-turn limit scales better.
 quote: "The clear trend is that SFT training does not induce any in-context exploration capability"; Table 2 row "RLEF 37.5 40.1".
 where: Sec 6.2, p32-35
11. Overthinking / compute control: unregularized RL pushes inference budget up. Proposes a discount rate gamma<1 and prompts such as "Work as quickly as possible" vs "Take as much time as needed".
 number: QwQ "generates up to 13 solutions in context" for simple questions.
 quote: "The Qwen QwQ model (Team, 2024) generates up to 13 solutions in context before providing a final answer."
 where: Sec 7.2.2, p42-43
12. Observed behaviours in frontier reasoners: o1 shows inconsistent flow, semantic backtracking and repetition. R1 shows heavy self-evaluation. Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking and QwQ show revision-style, whole-solution retries. Hypothesis only; the authors say they do not claim test-time tree search.
 quote: "we do not claim the model is implementing tree search at test time"
 where: Sec 4.4, p23-26
13. Reasoning models can hold the right answer in the trace and output a wrong final answer. The o1 showcase solution is incomplete.
 quote: "the single math example provided along with the announcement of the O1 model has an incomplete solution" and "Under a competitive setting this would likely receive 5/7 points"
 where: Sec 8.3.1, p48
14. Search cost: one MCTS tree with MC rollouts used up to 20M tokens, about $100.
 setup: Gemini 1.5 Pro (pass@128 = 6.25%, 8/128), one OpenAI-blog problem.
 quote: "a single tree uses up to 20 million inference tokens (a cost of ∼$100 per tree)"
 where: p22
15. PRM scaling (small): trained on 7,086 questions, about 97,000 trajectories; error falls with data; a big gap to the oracle verifier remains.
 quote: "the prediction error decreases as the size of the training data increases"
 where: Sec 5.2, p27
16. Tool-integrated reasoning (TIR) is more sample efficient. TIR trained on 100K problems vs CoT on 400K; "nearly double the accuracy" at low sample counts (AIMO_AMC, oracle verifier).
 quote: "Despite being fine-tuned on 25% as much data, the TIR model demonstrates superior scaling properties"
 where: Sec 8.3.5, p51
17. Big MATH dataset: 1,476,140 problems originally; 1,060,362 after base filter; 733,692 after strict filter (HARP, NuminaMath, Omni-MATH, OpenMathInstruct-2). NuminaMath: more than 42,500 duplicates of about 860,000; 89.7% have exactly one boxed answer.
 quote: "Total 1,476,140 1,060,362 733,692"
 where: Table 3, p46
18. Backtracking training (Ye et al. 2024b, 124M params): inserting incorrect steps at a 50% rate raised hard-math accuracy from 78% to 94% vs correct-only training. Small models only.
 quote: "a 50% rate of incorrect steps (objective in Equation 8) leads to an increase from 78% to 94% accuracy"
 where: p21
19. Async RL infra: shared-GPU-memory approach gives "40% improved throughput" over 3-step async. Trade-offs in tensor parallelism and KV cache.
 where: p47

LIMITS
- Authors' own: "Future work should validate the efficacy of our proposed pipeline." The pipeline (SFT on linearized search traces, then E-RL2 RL, plus the q-STaR objective) is proposed, not run end to end.
- The experiments are small or preliminary: 8B models, MATH only, one worked problem for synthetic MCTS/A* traces, a small PRM study. The "regret" metric is phrase-matching.
- The prompting study omits actual reasoning models (o1, R1) and gives no per-strategy accuracy numbers in the text. Accuracy appears only in Fig 25, drawn as lines.
- Much of the evidence is reused figures from other papers (Snell, Lehnert, Gandhi, Gehring, Kumar, Jones).
- The claim that o1 and R1 do search is inference from traces; their training is undisclosed. Dated: late 2024 models (o1, R1-lite, QwQ, Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking, Llama 3.1, Claude 3.5). The "open question" on RL-only reasoning was largely answered by later R1 work; do not treat it as current.
- The paper concedes the inference gains may vanish at larger scale: "the observed gains from additional inference might disappear at larger scales and training".
- It admits "evidence of emergent 'super'-reasoning ... appears weak".

BUILDS ON (as printed): Wei/CoT line; Merrill & Sabharwal 2023 (CoT complexity); Zelikman et al. 2022 (STaR), Singh et al. 2024; Zelikman 2024 (Quiet-STaR); Snell et al. 2024 and Brown et al. 2024 (test-time compute, repeated sampling); Lightman et al. 2023 (PRM800K); Cobbe et al. 2021 (verifiers); Wang et al. 2024 (MC value labels); Setlur et al. 2024a,b,c; Yao et al. 2023 (ToT); Hao et al. 2023 (RAP); Silver et al. 2018 / Jones 2021 (AlphaZero scaling); Gandhi et al. 2024 (Stream of Search); Lehnert et al. 2024; Kumar et al. 2024 (SCoRe); Qu et al. 2024; Gehring et al. 2024 (RLEF); Ye et al. 2024b; Zhang et al. 2024a/b; Duan et al. 2016 (RL2), Stadie et al. 2019 (E-RL2), Ghosh et al. 2021 (epistemic POMDP); Chen et al. 2024 (overthinking); Mahan et al. 2024; Kocsis & Szepesvari 2006 (UCT).

CODE: none. Equations worth keeping:
- Eq 14 (E-RL2): max over policy of E[ r(S_K, q) ], reward on the final episode only.
- Eq 15: max E[ r*(S,q) - beta * sum_t KL(pi_theta(z_{t+1}|Z_t,q) || pi_ref(...)) ].
- Eq 21 (discounted): gamma^{|Z|} r*(S,q) - beta * sum KL, gamma<1 (p43).
- Eq 11: v(S_t,q) = E over K=128 rollouts of r*, the MC value estimate (p22).

FIGURES (captions via figures.py):
- Fig 1 (p8): HARP accuracy and average tokens by difficulty; o1 uses far more tokens on hard problems. Core motivating picture.
- Fig 14 (p24): side-by-side o1 / R1 / Gemini 2.0 Flash Thinking traces with backtracking and verification highlighted. Shows what reasoning traces look like.
- Fig 25 (p37): tokens and accuracy by MATH level for each prompting strategy. The key figure for the prompting claims.
- Fig 22 (p33): RLEF scaling, turn limit 1 vs 3 vs 10, ground-truth vs random feedback.
- Fig 23 (p34): R1 inference scaling vs majority vote; parallel voting overtakes at high token budgets.
- Fig 27 (p43): hump-shaped accuracy vs compute under discounting; token length for "2+3=".
- Fig 9 (p18): log-linear inference-compute scaling for o1, Stream-of-Search and MAV-MCTS.
- Fig 10 (p20): sequential revisions beat parallel best-of-N.

PROBLEMS: No embedded instructions found in the text. Equations are garbled in the extraction (check the PDF before quoting any). Fig 24 (p36) text is not extractable. Fig 25 values are not readable from text; only the prose conclusions are citable. Table 5 numbers were read from the extraction and are reliable. A pypdf import failed in a second command (-I isolation, no pypdf in that interpreter), but the first extraction succeeded and was used for everything above. The extraction is saved at /tmp/xiang.txt (scratch only). Nothing in the repo was edited.
